content: A right-handed individual demonstrates greater dexterity and proficiency with their right hand compared to their left. This is evident in activities such as writing, personal grooming, cooking, and other daily tasks. Research indicates that approximately 85% to 90% of the global population is right-handed, while the majority of the remaining population is left-handed. A small subset of individuals possesses the ability to use both hands with equal skill, a trait referred to as ambidexterity. Neurological Basis of Right-Hand Dominance The motor functions of the right side of the body are controlled by the left hemisphere of the brain. Researchers hypothesize that the prevalence of right-handedness may be linked to functional differences between the brain's two hemispheres. However, while this asymmetry is well-documented, it does not definitively explain the underlying cause of right-hand dominance. Footedness and Ocular Dominance Being right-handed does not necessarily correlate with a preference for using the right foot. For example, in sports like football, many right-handed individuals prefer using their left foot. Similarly, people exhibit ocular dominance, where one eye is preferred over the other. There is only a weak correlation between being right-handed and having left-eye dominance. Theories Explaining Right-Hand Dominance 1. Warrior and Shield Theory: This theory suggests that right-handedness may have evolved due to the positioning of a warrior's shield and heart. Since the heart is slightly closer to the left side of the body, a right-handed warrior, who would hold a shield with their left hand and wield a weapon with their right, would be better equipped to protect their heart, increasing their chances of survival. 2. Brain Hemisphere Division of Labor: This theory posits that fine motor skills required for both speech and manual tasks are more efficiently managed by a single hemisphere of the brain. Since the left hemisphere typically governs both language and motor control for the right hand, this division of labor may have contributed to the predominance of right-handedness. Societal Implications of Right-Handedness Historically, many educational systems enforced right-handed writing, even among left-handed children. Cultural practices also reflect a preference for the right hand. For instance, in Hinduism, the right hand is used for auspicious and respectful activities such as eating, giving, receiving, and religious offerings, while the left hand is reserved for tasks considered inauspicious, such as personal hygiene. Similarly, in Islam, the right hand is used for eating, while the left is designated for cleaning oneself after using the bathroom. Technological and everyday tools are predominantly designed for right-handed users. Examples include refrigerators, scissors, microwaves, can openers, button-down shirts, computer mice, and kitchen mitts (which are often padded on one side only). Left-handed individuals face challenges in finding specialized items such as left-handed golf clubs. Historically, Japanese swords and modern cooking knives were crafted to favor right-handed users. Musical instruments, such as guitars, are also typically configured for right-handed players. In the military, rifles designed for right-shoulder firing have caused injuries to left-handed users due to spent cartridge casings striking their eyes or heads.
